levels.title: Capital stacks, remittance mechanics and renewal risk under real operating decisions

units.title: Building and reading a capital stack for a concrete operating need

lessons.title: The capital stack: what each layer claims, costs and controls
lessons.explanation: Your objective is to read a financing plan as a stack of layers competing for the same future cash rather than as a list of separate offers. Every layer can be described with five attributes: what it claims from future receipts, what it claims if value runs short, what control it imposes while outstanding, how long its payments run, and what it costs in dollars over that period. Federal programs show the range. SBA's 7(a) page describes a lender guarantee used for working capital, equipment, real estate and refinancing of existing business debt, with a maximum loan amount of $5 million and eligibility that includes being creditworthy with a reasonable ability to repay. The 504 page describes long-term fixed-rate financing of major fixed assets through Certified Development Companies (CDCs). The microloan page describes loans of up to $50,000 made through designated intermediary lenders. These are program descriptions, not a ranking, a comparison of which is cheaper, or evidence that any particular business would be approved. The structural teaching point is that a layer is not just a price: guarantee-supported amortizing debt, an equipment lease, a receivables facility and an advance repaid out of daily receipts all place different claims on the same operating account. A stack is coherent only when each layer's payments relate to what it financed, when the combined claims still leave room for payroll and suppliers, and when the owner can live with the control conditions. Nothing here is underwriting advice.
lessons.example: Anchor & Oak Kitchen plans $120,000 of uses: $55,000 of build-out, $30,000 of equipment and $35,000 of opening inventory. Its modeled stack is $40,000 of guarantee-supported term debt over 84 months at an assumed 9% annual rate, which is $643.56 a month, $54,059.30 in total and $14,059.30 of interest under those assumptions; $30,000 of equipment finance over 60 months at an assumed 8%, which is $608.29 a month, $36,497.51 in total and $6,497.51 of interest; a $20,000 advance at an assumed 1.35 factor, which is a $27,000 total remittance paid as $1,125 a week for 24 weeks and involves $7,000 of dollar cost inside roughly six months; $5,000 of owner cash; and $25,000 of build-out carried on 90-day supplier terms. Sources add to $120,000 and uses add to $120,000, so the plan balances arithmetically. The first month's financing outflow under these assumptions is $6,126.85, and $4,875 of it, or 79.57%, comes from the smallest layer. That layer is only 16.7% of the money raised yet supplies most of the early burden. Total modeled financing dollars are $27,556.81, which is 22.96% of uses. The factor is a multiplier applied to the amount purchased and must never be restated as an annual percentage rate; a compliant annualized figure would require the amounts and timing of value received and payments made.
lessons.question: Does the modeled $27,556.81 of financing cost on $120,000 of uses—about 23%—show that Anchor & Oak can carry this stack?
lessons.answer: No. A share of project size is not a payment schedule. The 24-week layer creates $4,875 of the $6,126.85 first-month outflow, and duration, collateral and control conditions still have to be tested against dated receipts.
lessons.distractor: Yes. At under 23% of total uses the financing dollars look modest for the project, so the stack can be treated as affordable.
lessons.correction: Total cost and payment timing are different quantities. A dollar total divided by project size describes the project, not any week's bank balance, and the short layer concentrates its claim into weeks when the build-out has produced nothing yet.

depth.definitions: A stack is the set of financing layers funding one plan. A claim is what a layer is entitled to receive, whether from receipts or from assets. Senior and subordinated describe the order in which claims are satisfied when value is insufficient; that order comes from the actual documents and applicable law, not from relative payment size. Duration is the period over which a layer's payments run, while asset life is the period over which the financed asset produces value. A guarantee-supported loan is made by a lender whose loss is partly guaranteed by a government agency; the borrower's obligation is not reduced to the unguaranteed portion. Gross advance is the face amount advanced or purchased, while net proceeds are what reaches the merchant after deductions, and a remittance is a payment applied to the obligation. Dollar cost is a difference in dollars under stated assumptions; an annualized percentage requires the amounts and timing of value received and payments made plus an applicable calculation method. A factor is not an APR, and this lesson computes no annualized value.
depth.mechanism: Sort the layers by duration, then by how quickly each financed item converts to cash. A build-out and inventory convert slowly; equipment converts over years through production; receivables convert in weeks. A layer paid over months cannot be supported by an asset that produces value over years unless other receipts subsidize it. Two further mechanisms matter. The first is control: shorter, higher-frequency products commonly require access to receipts, a filed security interest, or a personal guarantee, so an owner who is visibly paying down debt may already have pledged the accounts that fund payroll. The second is that program structure changes who carries the risk, not whether risk exists. SBA's eligibility language requires the business to be creditworthy and to show reasonable repayment ability, which is a condition the merchant must satisfy rather than a property the guarantee creates. Never present a program's existence as likely approval, because no provider outcome is predictable from a program description, and a guarantee does not remove the merchant's liability on the loan.
depth.secondExample: Contrast a duration-matched stack with a mismatched one for the same $85,000 tractor. Matched: a 60-month equipment loan at an assumed 8.5% annual rate costs $1,743.91 a month, $104,634.31 in total and $19,634.31 of interest, and the machine is expected to earn over those same five years. Mismatched: buying the same $85,000 through a 26-week purchase at an assumed 1.18 factor requires $100,300, or $3,857.69 a week, against an asset that cannot be converted to cash in six months. The mismatched version shows a lower total dollar figure and an unpayable weekly burden; the matched version shows a higher total and a payment the asset can plausibly service. The contrast shows why 'lower total cost' and 'better financing' are not the same statement. Neither structure is recommended, and both sets of terms are fictional.
depth.mistake: Two errors recur. The first is blending: quoting one blended cost as though the merchant experienced it evenly, which hides that the short layer takes most of the early cash. The second is treating new money as relief for old layers. If an advance arrives while existing remittances continue, two claims compete for the same receipts, which is the stacking pattern the FTC's staff perspective paper describes as a consequence of merchants being forced to renew in order to survive. Ask a stack question instead of a cost question: which layer is paid from which receipts in which weeks, and what happens if those receipts fall by a third? If the answer depends on a renewal that has not been approved, describe the stack as conditional rather than as solved. Do not advise a merchant to conceal an existing obligation or a filing, because concealment is the mechanism of fraud, not a financing strategy.
depth.application: Optional practice: build a five-column layer table (amount, net proceeds, duration, control conditions, claim on receipts) for one fictional plan, then write a two-sentence recommendation. Model response: 'The $120,000 plan balances, but the 24-week layer takes 79.57% of month-one financing outflow before the build-out earns anything, so I cannot call it affordable from the totals. May we verify the receipts calendar, each layer's control conditions and whether the equipment term could absorb more of the fit-out, and should the 90-day supplier terms be treated as a real obligation rather than free money?' Self-review: one row per layer; net proceeds distinguished from gross; no factor described as a rate; one non-debt alternative named; an explicit statement of what evidence would change the conclusion. Completing this exercise does not establish professional credit competence.
depth.summary: A capital stack is a claim-ordering problem with a timing problem inside it. Programs such as 7(a), 504 and microloans differ by use, size, term and who carries the risk, and those differences matter more than any single price. Carry the layer method into equipment replacement, an expansion or a seasonal build: name every layer, its net proceeds, its duration, its controls and the receipts that service it, then test the weakest link instead of the average.

lessons.title: Match the instrument to the use: duration, conversion and ownership
lessons.explanation: Your objective is to choose among financing instruments by matching three properties to the need: how long the need lasts, how the financed item converts back into cash, and who keeps ownership of the asset or the receivable. A delivery van converts over years through the routes it serves; a seasonal inventory build converts within one selling cycle; a receivable converts when the customer pays. The OCC's Asset-Based Lending booklet states that the primary source of repayment for revolving asset-based facilities is the conversion of collateral to cash over the company's business cycle, and it notes that lenders may also provide term financing for borrowers needing longer-term capital. That is the logic of matching: the facility's life is designed around the conversion period. The OCC's Lease Financing booklet separates products that look similar in a payment schedule but differ in ownership and residual risk, including the equipment finance agreement, the sale-leaseback, and leases treated as equivalent to loans. Two practical consequences follow. First, an instrument that keeps payments running after the financed value has been realized is a duration mismatch, not a bargain. Second, a product that transfers ownership of a receivable or an asset transfers risks and remedies with it, and whether the provider assumes customer credit risk depends on the actual agreement rather than on the product name. This lesson compares patterns, not approved products.
lessons.example: Ridgeline Delivery faces three needs at once. For a $60,000 van with a five-year service life, a 60-month equipment loan at an assumed 8% annual rate costs $1,216.58 a month, $72,995.02 in total and $12,995.02 of interest; financing the same van through a 26-week purchase at an assumed 1.15 factor would cost $69,000, or $2,653.85 a week, and $9,000 in dollars, but it would leave roughly four and a half years of useful van with no financing attached, inviting a renewal decision later. For a $45,000 seasonal inventory build repaid within about 22 weeks, a short facility at an assumed 1.12 factor costs $50,400, or $2,290.91 a week, and $5,400 in dollars; using a 48-month term loan at an assumed 9% instead costs $1,119.83 a month and $8,751.69 of interest, with 43 of those payments, totalling $48,152.56, falling after the inventory has already been sold. For $90,000 of invoices at 45-day terms, an 80% advance yields $72,000 now; pricing the transfer at an assumed 2% per 30 days makes 45 days cost $2,700, so the merchant receives a further $15,300 when the customer pays, whereas drawing $72,000 on a receivables line at an assumed 12% annual rate for 45 days costs $1,065.21 and keeps ownership of the invoice. Every rate and factor here is fictional, and none of these costs is an APR.
lessons.question: Ridgeline's controller asks which instrument is genuinely cheapest for the seasonal inventory. What is the defensible answer?
lessons.answer: Compare cost, duration and claims together: a short facility sized to the inventory cycle keeps payments inside the cycle, while the cheaper-sounding monthly loan leaves $48,152.56 of payments after the inventory is gone.
lessons.distractor: The 48-month term loan, because a monthly payment of $1,119.83 is smaller than a weekly payment of $2,290.91.
lessons.correction: Comparing a monthly figure with a weekly figure compares nothing. The loan's cost is spread over 48 months while the value it financed converts in about five, so the merchant carries payments, interest and refinancing risk for inventory that no longer exists.

depth.definitions: Duration matching means arranging a facility's payments to fall within the period over which the financed item produces cash. Conversion is the process by which collateral becomes spendable money, such as collecting a receivable or selling inventory. Recourse describes whether a provider can require repayment from the merchant if a customer fails to pay, and notification describes whether the customer is told to pay the provider directly; both are contractual choices rather than properties of a product name. A residual is the provider's estimate of an asset's value at the end of a lease term. Non-recourse, full-recourse and partial-recourse descriptions should be read in the executed documents, not the marketing page. Net proceeds are what the merchant actually receives after deductions, and dollar cost is a difference in dollars under stated assumptions.
depth.mechanism: Work from the conversion schedule outward. Identify when the money is needed, when it returns, and what happens if it returns late. A facility whose payments exceed the expected weekly conversion forces the merchant to subsidize it from unrelated receipts, which quietly converts operating cash into debt service. Term also shapes control. Longer amortizing facilities usually impose covenants and a blanket filing, while receivables arrangements may require collecting into a controlled account, and invoice transfer arrangements may give the provider rights against the merchant's customers. Where a facility is priced as a purchase rather than a loan, the total obligation is usually a fixed purchased amount, so repaying faster may not reduce what is owed; the FTC's staff perspective paper makes exactly this point about flat-fee products. Ask what happens when the conversion is late, whether a reserve or dilution adjustment applies, and whether the provider or the merchant bears a customer's failure to pay.
depth.secondExample: Take a print shop deciding between financing a $22,000 digital press over 60 months at an assumed 8.5% (which works out at $451.36 a month, $27,081.82 in total and $5,081.82 of interest) and leasing it under an assumed 60-month lease at $470 a month with a $3,000 end-of-term purchase option and a $1,500 return condition. The lease's nominally higher monthly figure is not automatically worse: the shop avoids capital cost and may keep operating cash, but it may also owe return-conditioning costs, mileage or usage limits may apply, and the asset is not the shop's unless it exercises the option. Compute total 60-month lease cost of $28,200 plus a $3,000 purchase option is $31,200 before any additional charges, versus $27,081.82 for the loan. The comparison changes with tax treatment and with what the shop does at the end of term, which is precisely why an ownership question cannot be answered by the monthly number alone. All terms are hypothetical.
depth.mistake: A frequent diagnostic error is comparing instruments on payment frequency: a $2,290.91 weekly figure is not 'bigger' than a $1,119.83 monthly figure until both are placed on the same calendar. Another error is assuming an inventory advance or a receivables facility is automatically cheaper because it is short; short facilities often carry the highest dollar cost per month of exposure, and the comparison must include how many weeks the merchant keeps the money. A third error is describing an invoice transfer as a loan or a loan as a sale of receipts. The label changes remedies, ownership and how a complaint or dispute would be handled, so state the mechanism the merchant is actually entering and route legal characterisation questions to qualified counsel rather than settling them in a sales call.
depth.application: Optional task: write a one-page matching memo for Ridgeline with a row per need, then a merchant-facing explanation. Model memo line: 'Van: 60-month amortising facility, duration matched, $12,995.02 of modeled interest. Inventory: 22-week facility, $5,400 of modeled dollar cost inside the cycle. Invoices: 80% advance, $2,700 modeled transfer cost over 45 days versus $1,065.21 on a drawn line that keeps ownership.' Model explanation: 'These are three different problems and I would not use one product for all three. Here is what changes in your bank account each week, what each provider can claim if something goes wrong, and what I still need to verify.' Self-review: same calendar for every option; net proceeds shown; ownership and recourse stated; one non-financing alternative; no invented rate; no claim that any option will be approved.
depth.summary: Instrument choice is a matching exercise before it is a price exercise. When duration, conversion and ownership line up with the need, the payment schedule has a source; when they do not, the merchant funds the gap from operations and inherits a renewal decision. Transfer the method to vehicle fleets, tooling, software subscriptions and purchase-order financing by asking what converts, when, and who carries the loss if it does not convert.

lessons.title: Advance and remittance mechanics: gross, net and the debit calendar
lessons.explanation: Your objective is to reconstruct what actually moves in a merchant's account under a revenue-linked advance, because the headline number is neither the cash received nor the amount repaid. Four quantities have to be separated. The amount purchased or advanced is the base the multiplier applies to. Deductions reduce what reaches the bank. Net proceeds are what the merchant can spend. Total remittance is the sum of the payments that will be collected over the schedule, which is where the cost sits. Around those four numbers sits the debit calendar: whether collections are a fixed amount, a stated percentage of defined receipts, or a fixed estimate that is later reconciled. California's commercial financing disclosure page states that, within its framework, providers must disclose the total amount of funds provided, the total dollar cost of financing, the term or estimated term, the method, frequency and amount of payments, and prepayment policies, and it notes that an annualized-rate item applied until January 1, 2024. Virginia's statute defines sales-based financing to include arrangements repaid as a percentage of sales or revenue and arrangements using a fixed payment with a true-up that adjusts to a percentage, and it treats a broker differently from a recipient. Those are jurisdiction-specific rules, not national ones, and they are reasons to obtain the provider's own disclosure rather than to construct an annualised figure yourself. A factor is a multiplier, not an interest rate and not an APR.
lessons.example: Harbor Threads accepts an offer whose stated advance amount is $50,000 with an assumed 1.32 factor. Deductions of $1,500 (a 3% origination deduction) and $500 in closing costs reduce net proceeds to $48,000. The total remittance is $66,000, collected as $2,750 a week over 24 weeks; the difference between remittance and net proceeds is $18,000, which is $750 for each week of the schedule. Now change the collection mechanism without changing the totals. If the agreement instead collects 12% of card settlements and card sales run $22,000 a week, the weekly amount is $2,640, and $66,000 takes exactly 25.0 weeks to collect rather than 24. If the schedule runs on business days instead of weekly, $66,000 over 120 debits is $550 a debit, and the money leaves more often even though the total is unchanged. Each variation changes the merchant's minimum balance and the payroll dates it can survive, which is why the cadence and not only the price belongs in the conversation. The $18,000 is a descriptive dollar difference under stated assumptions; it is not an APR, and calling it a 36% cost because $18,000 is 36% of $50,000 would be a category error.
lessons.question: The merchant is told '12% of card sales' in one place and a fixed $2,750 a week in another. Which figure governs, and why does the difference matter?
lessons.answer: The executed agreement governs. If the fixed estimate applies, $2,750 leaves weekly and any reconciliation is handled through the contract's process; if the percentage applies, $2,640 leaves at these volumes and the $66,000 takes 25.0 weeks instead of 24.
lessons.distractor: The $2,750 estimate always governs because estimated debits supersede percentage language in revenue-based agreements.
lessons.correction: Precedence is a contract question, not a default rule. The two mechanisms produce different weekly cash effects and different schedule lengths, so the merchant needs the written payment terms and the reconciliation clause before budgeting, not a reassurance that the amounts are 'about the same'.

depth.definitions: The advance or purchased amount is the base figure to which the factor is applied. A factor is a multiplier that converts that base into an expected total remittance. Deductions are amounts withheld or charged at or near funding, such as origination charges or closing costs. Net proceeds are what arrives in the merchant's account. Remittance is a collection applied against the obligation. A holdback or split is a proportion of defined receipts collected at the source, often from card settlements. An estimated debit is a scheduled fixed amount used before a reconciliation determines the contractual share. Reconciliation, also called a true-up, compares actual collections with the contractual definition and adjusts. Gross and net must never be presented interchangeably, and no factor should be described as an interest rate or an APR.
depth.mechanism: Trace the money in the order it moves. Funding first: base amount, deductions, net proceeds. Then the schedule: frequency, the source account or settlement file, the fallback if collections are insufficient, and whether the debit continues on days with no sales. Then the end: what happens when the purchased amount is remitted, whether any fee continues, and what the payoff figure would be on a specific date. Frequency is the most underweighted variable. Four weekly debits of $2,750 and 120 business-day debits of $550 are not remotely equivalent for a business whose suppliers are paid on the first and fifteenth, because the second structure drains cash on days when no receipts arrive and can produce a negative intraday balance even while the monthly total is unchanged. Confirm whether the provider collects from settlements at the point of sale, from a deposit account, or through a fixed schedule with reconciliation. When the source is a controlled or split arrangement, understand who can authorise a change and how quickly.
depth.secondExample: Contrast the same $50,000 offer when the merchant's cash arrives unevenly. Suppose receipts are $30,000 in peak weeks and $6,000 in slow weeks, and the agreement collects 12% of card settlements. Peak weeks contribute $3,600 and slow weeks $720, so the schedule self-adjusts and the $66,000 takes longer than 24 weeks overall. Now suppose instead that the agreement uses a fixed $2,750 weekly debit with an optional reconciliation the merchant must request with supporting records. In the slow weeks the merchant pays $2,750 against $6,000 of receipts, which is 45.8% of that week's money, and recovers any overpayment only through the reconciliation process. The two structures have identical totals and very different failure modes. The honest comparison states both, including which party must initiate the adjustment, what evidence is needed and how long an approved change takes to affect the bank account.
depth.mistake: The classic error is quoting gross borrowing next to net cash as if they were one number: a merchant told 'we funded $50,000' who received $48,000 has an unexplained $2,000 unless deductions are itemised. The second error is translating the multiplication into a rate. Dividing $18,000 by $50,000 and announcing 36% describes a multiplier over the whole schedule, not a rate over time, and dividing it by the 24 weekly periods to announce a weekly rate compounds a second error. The third error is assuming early repayment reduces the total; where the obligation is a fixed purchased amount, paying faster usually does not reduce it, which the FTC's staff perspective paper highlights as a source of borrower confusion. Correct all three by stating the base, the deductions, the net, the total, the calendar and the contractual treatment of early payment.
depth.application: Optional exercise: produce a one-page funding summary for a fictional merchant and a script for explaining it. Model summary: 'Base $50,000; deductions $2,000 (itemised); net proceeds $48,000; total remittance $66,000; $2,750 weekly for 24 weeks; remittance less net $18,000; percentage alternative at 12% of card sales would collect $2,640 a week at current volumes, about 25 weeks; reconciliation process to be confirmed in writing.' Model script: 'Two numbers matter to your bank account: what lands now and what leaves each week. Here they are, and here is what I still have to confirm before you decide.' Self-review: gross and net separated; every deduction named; cadence stated in dates; the factor described as a multiplier; no annualised value invented; the merchant's right to decline and to seek advice acknowledged.
depth.summary: An advance is a schedule as much as a price. The base amount, the deductions, the net proceeds, the total remittance and the collection cadence are five distinct facts, and the last of them often determines whether a correctly described deal is survivable. Transfer this discipline to subscription obligations, equipment rentals and any arrangement that collects from settlements: show what arrives, what leaves, on which days, and what happens if a collection day has no receipts.

lessons.title: Reconciliation in practice: definitions, evidence and status
lessons.explanation: Your objective is to operate a reconciliation clause as a documented process rather than as a promise of relief. Reconciliation, often called a true-up, compares what a provider actually collected with what the contract says it was entitled to collect. The FTC's staff perspective paper reports that two merchant cash advance providers themselves raised concerns at the agency's forum that some providers fail to perform promised true-ups, and it notes that failing to adjust payments when sales fall could be unlawful. Virginia's statute defines sales-based financing to include a fixed-payment arrangement with a true-up that adjusts the payment to a percentage of sales or revenue. Those two sources frame the discipline: the right to an adjustment comes from the contract language, and the value of that right depends on evidence, process and timing. Three things get confused. A calculation is arithmetic under an assumed definition. A contractual entitlement is what the documents support. Settlement is what has actually been credited or refunded to the merchant. This lesson keeps those on three lines, because a pending adjustment is not spendable cash and cannot fund a payroll date that arrives first. The numbers below are fictional and assume one particular definition of the receipts base.
lessons.example: Cedar & Slate Interiors has an agreement that collects 9% of 'eligible settled receipts', defined as settled card receipts plus settled customer deposits, less documented refunds and chargebacks. In one week, card receipts settle at $31,000 and customer deposits at $14,000. Documented refunds are $2,500, so the receipts base is $42,500 and the contractual share is $3,825. The provider's fixed estimated debit for the week was $4,250, so the merchant was over-collected by $425. Over a documented eight-week period the same pattern produces $3,400 of over-collection, which is a scenario for tracking a potential adjustment under this definition rather than proof that a refund is owed. The definition is doing real work: if the provider computed the share on gross settled receipts without deducting the refunds, the base would be $45,000, the share $4,050 and the weekly difference $200, which is $1,600 over eight weeks. The same events therefore support an adjustment claim of either $3,400 or $1,600 depending on which description of the base is correct, and only the executed agreement settles that question. Every figure assumes funding has already occurred and prices are as stated; no refund or credit is assumed to have been received.
lessons.question: May the owner treat the eight-week $3,400 as available cash and plan the quarter around it?
lessons.answer: No. Track it as a pending adjustment with a recorded status until the actual refund or debit credit appears on the bank record, and reconcile the timing against the owner's obligations.
lessons.distractor: Yes. Once the arithmetic is documented the provider is obliged to pay it, so it can be counted as cash in the forecast.
lessons.correction: Documented arithmetic establishes the size of a difference under a definition; it does not establish entitlement, timing or implementation. An adjustment may arrive as a refund, a credit against future debits or another agreed treatment, and each has a different cash date.

depth.definitions: Eligible receipts are whatever the contract's definition includes, which may exclude cash sales, taxes, tips, certain processors or disputed items, and may or may not be reduced by refunds, chargebacks or processor fees. A receipts base is the figure to which the percentage is applied. An estimated debit is the scheduled amount collected before reconciliation. An adjustment is the amount by which collections and entitlement diverged. A refund returns value; a credit reduces a future collection; a debit reduction changes the amount taken on specified dates. Implementation is the point at which the merchant's bank record changes. Processing lag is the interval from the triggering collection to the implemented change. Notice provisions govern how a request must be made, and supporting records are whatever the process requires, commonly settlement statements and documented refunds.
depth.mechanism: Build a reconciliation ledger with one row per period and these columns: period, receipts base as computed, excluded items with reasons, contractual share, amount actually debited, difference, evidence attached, submission date, acknowledgement date, outcome and implementation date. Each column answers a different question, and a row is not complete until the outcome column is filled. Then overlay the merchant's payment dates. If relief will arrive as a credit against future debits, forecast lower outflows on the confirmed dates instead of inventing an immediate deposit. If it will arrive as a refund, record the expected bank date separately. Never enter the same adjustment twice; a refund and a credit are alternative mechanisms, not cumulative benefits. Keep fee lines and old obligations outside the reconciliation so that the same dollar is not reconciled against two claims. Where the provider's practice diverges from the written process, preserve records through authorised channels and route the dispute to servicing, compliance or counsel as appropriate.
depth.secondExample: Contrast a contract with automatic percentage collection against one with a fixed debit and a request-based true-up. Under automatic percentage collection, a week with $12,000 of eligible receipts generates a $1,080 collection at 9% with no separate action, so the merchant's outflow falls with receipts; the trade-off is that the obligation takes longer to complete and may extend into a season when the merchant wanted it finished. Under the request-based structure in the first example, collections stay at $4,250 until the merchant produces evidence and the provider implements a change, so a slow fortnight can produce a real shortfall before any correction. Neither structure is inherently honest or dishonest, and a provider operating the second structure correctly is not failing the merchant. The point is that the merchant must know which one they signed, who initiates the adjustment and how long it takes, because those facts determine whether a difficult month becomes a liquidity event.
depth.mistake: The harmful script is 'reconciliation means you can always afford it', which converts a contractual process into a solvency guarantee. Diagnose the claim by asking four questions: who initiates the request, what evidence is required, how long review takes, and how an approved adjustment reaches the account. If any answer is unknown, the assurance is unsupported. A second error is instructing an owner to block or reverse debits unilaterally; this course does not advise defaulting, evading payment authorisations or altering records, and any dispute about amounts, authorisations or contracts belongs with authorised servicing staff and qualified professionals. A third error is treating an acknowledgement email as implementation: an acknowledged request has not changed a single bank balance.
depth.application: Optional task: draft a servicing enquiry and an internal cash note. Model enquiry: 'Please confirm the definition of the receipts base, whether documented refunds are deducted, the evidence format you require, the status of our request, whether an approved difference is treated as a refund or a credit, and the date any change would take effect.' Model cash note: 'Under our reading of the definition the weekly difference is $425, or $3,400 over eight weeks, but we will not treat an unconfirmed adjustment as available cash and we will not double-count a credit and a refund.' Self-review: calculation separated from entitlement and from implementation; excluded items listed; evidence identified; no unauthorised account action recommended; records retained in an approved system; no promise of an outcome; decisions left with the owner and, where needed, qualified advisers.
depth.summary: Reconciliation is a process with a definition, an evidence standard, a submission route and an implementation step. The merchant's protection is not the presence of the word in the contract but the ability to operate it. Transfer this method to rebate programmes, insurance reimbursements and landlord credits: compute the difference, prove the basis, track the status, and only then change the cash forecast.

lessons.title: Guarantees, liens and jurisdiction: who can reach which assets
lessons.explanation: Your objective is to identify the non-price terms that decide what happens if a deal goes wrong, and to see that the same economics produce different paperwork in different places. Three mechanisms matter. A personal guarantee makes an individual answerable for a business obligation, usually up to a stated amount or without limit, and it is common: the Federal Reserve's 2026 Report on Employer Firms reports that, among firms that had debt, 59% used a personal guarantee. A security interest gives a provider a claim on specified assets, and perfection normally requires filing: Uniform Commercial Code section 9-310 states that, except for enumerated exceptions, a financing statement must be filed to perfect a security interest, while section 9-324 gives a purchase-money security interest in goods other than inventory priority over a conflicting interest if it is perfected when the debtor receives possession or within 20 days afterwards. A blanket filing covering all assets therefore does not automatically defeat the lender that financed the machine. Third, jurisdiction changes the rules: Utah requires providers to register before engaging in commercial financing with a Utah resident and imposes disclosure duties; Virginia exempts financial institutions, providers doing no more than five transactions in twelve months and single transactions over $500,000; California itemises required disclosures; New York drafted its own definitions and process. Two transactions with identical costs can therefore differ in registration, disclosure, filing and remedy. None of this is legal advice, and characterisation of a given arrangement is a question for qualified counsel.
lessons.example: Northgate Machine Works has a $75,000 advance outstanding and a $30,000 equipment balance, so $105,000 of claims exist. Appraised equipment is $60,000, receivables $25,000 and other assets $10,000, giving $95,000 of asset value before discounts for collection costs and realisable-value haircuts. The pledge therefore exceeds appraised value by $10,000. The advance agreement carries a personal guarantee limited to $40,000 and a blanket filing; the equipment lender's purchase-money claim on the machine is the kind of interest section 9-324 addresses. Mid-way through the schedules, if the advance is down to $45,000 outstanding, total claims are $75,000 against $95,000 of appraised value, a $20,000 margin. That movement shows why coverage is a moving number: the same business looks exposed in month one and covered in month nine, and neither snapshot proves what a court or a workout would produce. The arithmetic also shows why a limited guarantee of $40,000 is not equivalent to a claim on $40,000 of assets: enforceability, priority, filing accuracy, notice and the contract's default provisions all sit between the document and any collection. All figures and businesses are fictional.
lessons.question: Does the $10,000 arithmetic shortfall mean Northgate's owner should expect a personal demand under the guarantee?
lessons.answer: No. The arithmetic compares pledged claims with appraised collateral value. Whether a guarantee can be enforced, by whom and for how much depends on the executed documents, the applicable law and the facts of any default, and belongs with qualified counsel.
lessons.distractor: Yes. Once claims exceed asset value the guarantee is automatically triggered and the owner should plan to pay the difference personally.
lessons.correction: Collateral coverage and guarantee enforcement are different questions. Priority rules such as section 9-324 can leave a blanket filer behind a purchase-money lender, appraised values are not sale proceeds, and enforcement follows contractual and legal conditions rather than arithmetic alone.

depth.definitions: A guarantee is a separate promise to answer for another party's obligation; it may be limited by amount, capped by time, or supported by a separate collateral pledge. A security interest is a right in collateral that secures payment. Attachment is the point at which the interest becomes enforceable between the parties; perfection is the additional step, usually filing, that protects it against other claimants. A financing statement (often called a UCC-1) is the filed record; section 9-515 provides that it is effective for five years and lapses unless a continuation statement is filed, and that a continuation may be filed only within six months before that expiration. A blanket filing covers a broad range of assets, sometimes described as all assets, including after-acquired ones. Subordination is a contractual agreement to place one claim behind another. Registration and disclosure statutes such as Utah's and Virginia's are provider-facing requirements, not consumer protections the merchant can self-execute.
depth.mechanism: Read a deal backwards from default. First, which assets can be reached, and is the claim specific or blanket? Second, is that claim perfected, and when? A purchase-money lender that perfects within the statutory window can sit ahead of an earlier blanket filer on the financed goods, so the merchant who believes 'the first filer wins everything' will misread the exposure. Third, what personal exposure exists, in what amount, and can it be capped in negotiation? Fourth, what does the contract define as default, and how much notice or cure is allowed? Fifth, who holds the receivables: if collections are routed to a controlled account, the merchant's operating liquidity depends on that arrangement regardless of the headline balance. Finally, track filing and release administration: a satisfied obligation with an unreleased filing can obstruct future financing until the filing is terminated or lapses, and a lapsed filing has specific consequences under section 9-515. Verify filings through the appropriate state office rather than relying on a provider's summary, and do not advise a merchant to hide an existing obligation: presenting false information to a creditor is fraud, not negotiation.
depth.secondExample: Compare two merchants with the same $75,000 advance. Merchant A borrows in a jurisdiction where the provider must register and deliver itemised disclosures before the transaction is finalised, and the agreement caps the guarantee at $40,000. Merchant B, in a state with a five-transaction exemption and an over-$500,000 threshold, deals with a provider that is outside those particular requirements, and the agreement contains an unlimited personal guarantee. The dollar cost can be identical while the consequences of a bad year are not: in one case the owner's exposure is bounded and documented, in the other it is open-ended. A third merchant operates in a state where a sales-based transaction must be disclosed with estimated payments, and finds that the estimate is later reconciled. Same product family, three different sets of duties and risks. The comparison is a reason to ask what regime governs a specific offer, not a reason to assume one state's rules travel.
depth.mistake: A common but damaging shortcut is telling an owner that a personal guarantee 'never gets enforced' or that a blanket filing 'doesn't really matter'. The FTC's 2022 settlement with RAM Capital Funding concerned, among other allegations, demanding personal guarantees and upfront fees after representing they would not require them, providing less funding than promised and debiting more than promised. The lesson is that material claims must match the documents, so a broker who says 'no guarantee required' before reading the contract has created exactly that exposure. A second error is assuming a filing is automatically released on payoff; releases and terminations require action, and a stale filing can block the next lender. A third is advising a merchant to conceal an obligation or a filing from a new provider. Correct all three by describing the actual documents, verifying filings, and routing enforcement and characterisation questions to counsel.
depth.application: Optional task: build a non-price term sheet for a fictional deal with four rows (guarantee amount and type, specific versus blanket collateral, filing status and release process, default and cure terms) and draft the client-facing explanation. Model explanation: 'The price is one page of this decision. Here is what the agreement lets the provider reach, here is what the owner personally promises, here is what is filed today and how it gets released, and here is what I could not verify. Please have counsel read the guarantee before you sign.' Self-review: no claim that a guarantee will not be enforced; no advice to conceal or misrepresent; filing verification named; jurisdiction-specific items flagged as requiring compliance review; the merchant's option to decline or seek alternatives preserved.
depth.summary: Non-price terms decide the downside. Guarantees create personal exposure, filings determine who reaches which assets and in what order, and jurisdiction determines the duties a provider owes before and after funding. Transfer the method to leases, purchase-money equipment, receivables facilities and renewals: read default backwards, verify filings at the source, and treat any promise about what a guarantee means as a question for counsel rather than for a sales conversation.

questions.prompt: A broker proposes a $20,000 advance to a merchant whose existing revenue-linked remittance of $2,750 a week still has ten weeks to run, and describes the new cash as 'breathing room'. Both obligations collect from the same card settlements and debits total $5,350 a week while the new net proceeds are $38,500. What must the layer analysis show before this is called relief?
questions.answer: Both claims on the same receipts, the $5,350 combined weekly outflow and the roughly 7.2 weeks of net proceeds that would cover it, plus whether the existing agreement permits the new obligation.
questions.distractor: The combined weekly figure of $3,350, because the new remittance partly offsets the old one and only the difference leaves the account.
questions.correction: Nothing offsets: two providers collect separately, so gross debits are $5,350 a week, and $38,500 of net proceeds covers about 7.2 weeks of them. Whether stacking is permitted is a contract question, and calling the pattern relief before checking it misstates the liquidity.

questions.prompt: A wholesaler funds a $70,000 refrigeration unit expected to run for twelve years using a 26-week product at an assumed 1.2 factor, arguing that its $84,000 total is lower than a longer amortising facility's total. What is the strongest correction?
questions.answer: Compare instruments by duration fit: a six-month schedule attached to a twelve-year asset leaves the merchant financing replacements and renewals long before the asset stops producing value.
questions.distractor: The 26-week product is superior because a lower total dollar cost always indicates a better financing decision.
questions.correction: Total dollars ignore when the value appears. The refrigeration unit earns over twelve years while the schedule collects in six months, so the merchant may need further financing while still using the same asset, adding renewal and refinancing risk even when the summed dollars look smaller.

questions.prompt: A funding statement says the merchant was advanced $50,000, but $48,000 arrived and no deductions are itemised. The merchant asks what to do before the first debit. Which response is correct?
questions.answer: Ask for the itemised deductions that reconcile $50,000 to $48,000, and confirm in writing the total remittance, the cadence and the treatment of early payment.
questions.distractor: Treat the difference as a rounding or processing matter, since the scheduled weekly payment is already fixed and known.
questions.correction: Unitemised deductions leave the merchant unable to verify the base, the net proceeds or the total obligation, and the first debit does not answer those questions. Requesting the itemisation is a documentation request, not an accusation of misconduct.

questions.prompt: Under one reading of the receipts definition a merchant was over-collected by $425 a week, and under another reading the over-collection is $200 a week, because the provider did not deduct documented refunds. What determines the correct figure, and how should it be used?
questions.answer: The executed agreement's definition of eligible receipts determines the figure; the computed amount is recorded as a pending adjustment until a refund or credit is actually implemented and seen in the bank record.
questions.distractor: The larger figure governs, because a merchant should always claim the highest defensible number and reconcile later if the provider disagrees.
questions.correction: A larger claim is not more accurate arithmetic. The receipts base comes from the contract, and even the correct figure is only a calculation until the provider implements the adjustment; forecasting it as cash would invent liquidity.

questions.prompt: A provider's marketing says no personal guarantee and no blanket filing. The document presented for signature contains a limited guarantee and a filing covering all assets after acquired property. The merchant also has an existing purchase-money equipment loan. What should the adviser do?
questions.answer: Point to the specific contradictions between the marketing and the documents, have counsel review the guarantee and filing, and check with the filing office whether the purchase-money lender's interest was perfected within the statutory window.
questions.distractor: Reassure the merchant that the guarantee will not be enforced and that the earlier filing takes priority over everything filed later.
questions.correction: Contradictory representations are precisely the conduct enforcement actions address, so the documents control. Priority is not determined by filing order alone: a purchase-money interest perfected on time can sit ahead of an earlier blanket filing, and release, lapse and enforcement questions need counsel and the filing office, not reassurance.

units.title: Pricing under funding cost, renewal pressure and honest selling

lessons.title: Funding cost inside unit margin: what the remittance does to contribution
lessons.explanation: Your objective is to place the financing obligation inside the merchant's unit economics, so that a payment is judged against the contribution that pays it rather than against revenue. Contribution per unit is selling price less the variable costs incurred to make and deliver that unit. Financing obligations are largely fixed in amount and date: they are paid whether or not the units are sold, and they are paid from total contribution alongside rent, wages and tax. That makes the useful calculations different from what many sales conversations imply. First, how many units of contribution does the weekly remittance consume? Second, what percentage of planned contribution does the obligation absorb, leaving how much for everything else? Third, how does that change if the merchant discounts price or if product mix shifts to lower-margin items? SBA's 7(a) eligibility language requires a business to demonstrate reasonable ability to repay, and the OCC's asset-based lending booklet discusses financial and repayment capacity analysis in the same spirit: repayment ability is a claim on the whole business, not a property of one profitable order. Financing cost must not be attributed to a single unit's margin to argue that the unit 'pays for itself', and unit data must come from the merchant's own records rather than from an assumed margin. The figures below are fictional and the proceeds are illustrative, not offers.
lessons.example: Northline Print has a contribution of $16 per unit, from a $42 selling price less $26 of variable cost. Its revenue-linked remittance is $2,750 a week. Dividing the remittance by contribution gives 171.875, so 172 units of contribution cover the payment; 171 units would provide $2,736, which is $14 short. If competitive pressure pushes the price to $39 and variable cost holds, contribution falls to $13 and the same remittance needs 211.538, that is 212 units, with 211 units providing $2,743. At the planned volume of 350 units the weekly contribution is $5,600, so the remittance absorbs 49.11% of contribution, an effective $7.86 of financing load per unit sold. Add $3,200 a week of fixed operating cost, and the business must sell 371.875, that is 372 units, to cover financing and fixed cost together, providing $5,952 against $5,950 of obligations. Against a capacity of 500 units, headroom is 128 units, or 25.6%. Nothing in the arithmetic says the payment is unaffordable; it says the payment removes about half of contribution before wages, rent and tax are considered, which is the fact the owner needs in order to decide.
lessons.question: The owner proposes to attribute the remittance to the highest-margin product line and says that line 'covers the financing on its own'. What is wrong with that reasoning?
lessons.answer: The remittance is a fixed claim paid from total contribution on set dates. Attributing it to one line ignores that the line may not sell in the weeks the payment falls and that other costs also draw on the same contribution.
lessons.distractor: Nothing, provided the attributed line's total contribution exceeds the remittance over the whole schedule, because the schedule and the sales period are the same length.
lessons.correction: Length of schedule and timing of sales are different facts. A line whose contribution arrives in a later season cannot pay a debit in a slow month, and contribution must still fund fixed operating costs and tax. The correct statement is how many units of contribution the payment consumes in a given week and what remains.

depth.definitions: Contribution is revenue less variable costs under a stated boundary. Fixed costs do not change with volume within a range. The contribution margin ratio expresses contribution as a share of revenue. Break-even units for a fixed obligation equal that obligation divided by contribution per unit, rounded up because a partial unit cannot be sold. Financing load per unit is the period's financing obligation divided by units sold in the period, an average that falls as volume rises and rises as volume falls, even though the obligation itself does not move. Distinguish a unit contribution from a project contribution: the first supports weekly obligations, the second tests whether a specific activity is worth doing. A factor remains a multiplier and is not an APR; no annualised figure is calculated here.
depth.mechanism: Layer three coverage tests rather than one. The first covers financing alone. The second covers financing plus fixed operating cost. The third covers financing plus fixed cost plus a reserve for tax, seasonality and error, which is the test that usually reveals how thin a plan is. Then stress the two inputs that move most: price and volume. A discount is not merely a revenue reduction; because variable costs are unchanged, it removes contribution at the full discounted amount, and the required units rise disproportionately. Mix changes do the same thing quietly: a shift from a $16-contribution line to a $13-contribution line raises the required volume by about 23% for the same payment. Finally, insist on the merchant's own records for price, variable cost and volume; an assumed margin imported from an industry average will make an unaffordable obligation look comfortable, and the OCC's borrower-analysis discussion of repayment capacity assumes verified information rather than a favourable illustration.
depth.secondExample: Contrast a service business with high contribution and low fixed cost against a distributor with low contribution and high fixed cost, both carrying the same $2,750 weekly remittance. The service business sells a $900 project with $300 of direct labour and materials, giving $600 of contribution: fewer than five projects a week cover the payment, and one large project can cover a fortnight. The distributor sells a $120 case with $104 of cost, giving $16 of contribution: about 172 cases are needed each week, and a two-week supplier shutdown that empties the warehouse pushes the required volume above what the market will absorb. Same payment, same arithmetic method, entirely different fragility. That contrast is why a financing recommendation should be expressed in the merchant's own unit terms and why a distributor with slow turn deserves a more conservative structure or a smaller obligation rather than a lower headline payment.
depth.mistake: The most common error is converting the merchant's revenue into a false sense of coverage: 'you bill $60,000 a month, so $2,750 a week is nothing.' Revenue includes variable costs and pass-through items, and the obligation is paid from contribution. Diagnose that claim by asking for the contribution figure and the units required. A second error is comparing the financing payment with profit after tax and declaring it affordable, when the payment falls on dates regardless of when profit is realised. A third is treating the financing load per unit as a cost of goods, which would misstate gross margin and make future pricing decisions worse. The correction in every case is the same: state the obligation, state the contribution, state the units required, state the dates, and show what changes if price or volume moves.
depth.application: Optional task: compute the coverage tests for a fictional merchant and write a two-sentence recommendation in unit terms. Model response: 'At $16 of contribution per unit this $2,750 weekly obligation consumes 172 units, and with $3,200 of weekly fixed cost you need 372 units of your 500-unit capacity, which is 25.6% headroom before tax and seasonality. If the discount holds at $39, the requirement rises to 212 units for financing alone, so I would not recommend the payment without seeing two months of your actual unit records.' Self-review: each figure traceable to the merchant's records; rounding up for requirements; a stated volume assumption; a stress case; no annualised cost invented; no guarantee of approval or outcome.
depth.summary: A financing obligation is a fixed claim on variable contribution. The useful answer to 'can the business afford this?' is a unit count, a percentage of contribution and a stressed version, not a comparison of the payment with revenue. Transfer the method to lease payments, software subscriptions and a new hire: state the fixed claim, divide by contribution, and check the headroom against the season.

lessons.title: Renewal and refinancing risk: what a new round costs after the first one
lessons.explanation: Your objective is to evaluate a renewal or refinance as a lifecycle decision rather than as a fresh offer. A renewal is usually presented with attractive terms: a new net deposit, a slightly different factor, a lower weekly payment. The lifecycle question is what the merchant pays in total across both rounds, what the new money actually adds, and what remains when the shorter phase ends. Three mechanics drive the answer. First, the outstanding balance of the original obligation is a claim that must be satisfied or carried; if it is paid off from new proceeds, the merchant's spendable amount is reduced accordingly, and if it is not paid off, two claims collect at once. Second, the total purchased amount of the new round is generally fixed, so paying faster may not reduce it, a point the FTC's staff perspective paper raises about flat-fee products and borrower expectations of early-repayment savings. Third, the payment tail: the obligations that remain after any promotional phase means the merchant's cash position in later weeks is a distinct risk from the cash position today. The OCC's Lease Financing booklet discusses renewals, extensions and off-lease property precisely because end-of-term decisions carry valuation and residual risk, and the same reasoning applies to any staged facility. Renewals also interact with documentation: an old filing may need to be terminated, an old account may need a documented stop, and the new agreement may restrict further obligations. Whether a payoff is permitted, and whether a new claim may legally sit alongside an old one, are contract and legal questions.
lessons.example: Brightwater Landscaping's original facility had a $50,000 advance amount, a 1.32 factor, a $66,000 total remittance and $2,750 weekly debits over 24 weeks. At the end of week 14 the merchant has paid 14 times $2,750, or $38,500, and $27,500 of remittance remains. A renewal is offered at week 14: a $40,000 advance amount, a $1,500 deduction, so net proceeds of $38,500, a 1.30 factor and a $52,000 total remittance collected as $2,600 a week for 20 weeks. If the remaining $27,500 is paid off from the proceeds, the merchant's new spendable cash is $11,000. Across the whole lifecycle the merchant will have paid $38,500 plus $52,000, or $90,500, compared with $66,000 under the original schedule alone: $24,500 of additional future payments to obtain $11,000 more now. That sentence is the honest description, and the $24,500 must not be renamed as an APR or as a percentage rate, because a compliant annualised figure would require the amounts and timing of value received and payments made under an applicable method. If instead the $27,500 is not paid off, both obligations collect: $2,750 plus $2,600 is $5,350 a week, and the $38,500 of net proceeds covers about 7.2 weeks of that combined outflow. Every figure is fictional and assumes no fees beyond the stated deduction.
lessons.question: The renewal's weekly payment is $2,600 against the original $2,750, so the broker calls it a saving. Which statement is defensible?
lessons.answer: The weekly payment is lower, but the schedule is longer and the merchant pays $24,500 more in total to obtain $11,000 of new cash, so the lower payment is not evidence of a lower cost.
lessons.distractor: The renewal is cheaper because a 1.30 factor is below the original 1.32 factor and the weekly payment is $150 smaller.
lessons.correction: Two rounds produce two obligations. The lifecycle total of $90,500 compares with $66,000 for the original schedule, and the $38,500 of new proceeds includes $27,500 used to extinguish the old balance. A lower factor on a smaller gross amount does not offset the added round.

depth.definitions: A renewal extends or replaces an obligation, usually with new proceeds and new terms. A refinance replaces one obligation with another, often from a different provider. Payoff is the amount needed to extinguish an existing obligation on a given date, which may differ from a pro-rata figure depending on the contract. The payment tail is the stream of obligations remaining after an earlier phase ends. A lifecycle total sums all payments across all rounds under stated assumptions. Incremental cash is the new spendable amount after any payoff and deductions. Stacking is the coexistence of multiple obligations drawing on the same receipts without the earlier claim being satisfied. An early-payoff discount, if any, must be read in the executed contract because many revenue-linked products are structured as purchases of a fixed amount.
depth.mechanism: Map both rounds on one calendar. Mark each deduction, deposit, payoff, debit and the date the old obligation is expected to end. Then compute three quantities: the lifecycle total of payments, the incremental cash the merchant can spend now, and the burden in the weeks after any payoff or promotional phase. Stress-test the payoff: if the old provider's debit does not stop when expected, the merchant pays both, which is the pattern behind stacking complaints. Check the documentation chain: a termination statement for an old filing, a written stop of an old authorisation, confirmation that an old account has zero balance, and notice of any restriction on new obligations in either contract. If a refinance is used to escape a reconciliation dispute, treat that as a signal rather than a solution; the FTC's staff paper notes that providers failing to perform promised true-ups is itself a concern, and replacing a disputed obligation with a larger one can simply move the problem forward.
depth.secondExample: Consider a genuine replacement: a term loan of $60,000 replaced by another lender at the same outstanding balance with a lower monthly payment over a longer term. The payoff is verified, the old filing is terminated and the old debits stop, so only one claim collects. The monthly payment falls, but the merchant will pay more months, and the total interest may be higher than finishing the original loan. Contrast a renewal that raises available cash: the merchant receives genuine new money, but the lifecycle total rises and the schedule extends, which is a fair trade only if the new money funds something that produces a return. In both cases the test is the same three quantities, and the honest answer depends on whether the merchant needs cash now badly enough to buy it with later obligations. Neither path is guaranteed to be approved, and no refinancing should be described as certain to complete.
depth.mistake: The reassuring script is 'your payment drops, so you are better off', which compares one week of two different schedules. Diagnose it by asking for the lifecycle total, the amount of proceeds consumed by payoff and the weeks remaining after the new schedule's final debit. A second error is presenting a new factor as an improvement when the gross amount has changed, since factors apply to different bases. A third and more serious error is arranging a new obligation without disclosing the existing one. The FTC's 2022 settlement action involving RAM Capital Funding alleges, among other things, funding shortfalls and misrepresented personal guarantees and fees; presenting an incomplete picture is the conduct that enforcement addresses, so disclose existing claims and let the provider decide under its own policy.
depth.application: Optional task: prepare a renewal comparison sheet and the client conversation. Model sheet: 'Original: $50,000 advance, 1.32 factor, $66,000 total over 24 weeks. At week 14: $38,500 paid, $27,500 remaining. Renewal: $40,000 advance, net $38,500, 1.30 factor, $52,000 total over 20 weeks. If payoff is $27,500, new spendable cash is $11,000 and the lifecycle total is $90,500 against $66,000.' Model conversation: 'The weekly number goes down and the total goes up. Here is what you would spend to get $11,000 today, here is how the last twenty weeks look, and here is what I need confirmed about the old account before you decide either way.' Self-review: lifecycle total shown; payoff verified rather than assumed; both stacking scenarios priced; no annualised figure invented; no promise that a renewal or refinance will be approved; the option to decline included.
depth.summary: Renewals are judged across rounds, not within them. The three quantities that decide the question are the lifecycle total, the incremental cash actually available after payoff, and the burden after the earlier phase ends. Transfer the method to lease end-of-term options, equipment trade-ins and debt consolidations: verify extinguishment, price the tail, and describe the trade in dollars rather than in payment size.

lessons.title: Seasonal receipts and cadence fit: fixed schedules versus share-of-receipts structures
lessons.explanation: Your objective is to compare a fixed repayment calendar with a share-of-receipts structure against a business whose revenue is seasonal, and to state the trade-off honestly rather than selling flexibility as safety. Two structures are common. In the fixed structure, a set amount leaves on set dates regardless of trading, sometimes with a reconciliation process that the merchant must initiate. In the share-of-receipts structure, collections equal a defined percentage of defined receipts, so the amount falls when sales fall and rises when sales rise. The second is often described as seasonally friendly, and in one sense it is: it cannot demand a percentage larger than the contract states out of receipts the contract defines. But because the total purchased amount is generally fixed, slower collection means a longer obligation, so the merchant trades a lower payment now for a tail that extends further into a period when they wanted to be finished. The OCC's asset-based lending booklet frames lending around the conversion of collateral to cash over the company's business cycle, which is exactly the variable that seasonality distorts. Jurisdictional disclosure rules recognise the uncertainty too: California's framework requires the term or estimated term and the method, frequency and amount of payments to be disclosed, and Virginia's statute treats a fixed payment with a true-up as sales-based financing. The practical work is to decide which risk the owner prefers and can survive: a demand that continues through a slow month, or an obligation that outlasts the season. Figures below are fictional.
lessons.example: Windrose Garden Center has a 24-week schedule of $2,750 a week, a $66,000 total remittance and net proceeds of $48,000. Its receipts average $85,000 a month in the growing season, which is $19,615.38 a week, and $35,000 a month in deep winter, which is $8,076.92 a week. Against receipts, the fixed remittance takes 14.02% of the growing-season week and 34.05% of the winter week: the same payment, more than double the share. If the schedule begins in late summer, weeks 17 to 24 fall in the winter trough, and eight weeks of $2,750 is $22,000, which is 45.83% of the merchant's net proceeds from the advance. Under a share structure collecting 8% of receipts, the growing-season weeks generate $1,569.23 a week, so 16 weeks collect $25,107.69 and leave $40,892.31 to collect; in winter the same 8% yields $646.15 a week, and $40,892.31 at that rate takes about 63.3 more weeks. The total remains $66,000 in this illustration, so the merchant pays the same amount, spread over roughly eighteen months instead of six, and keeps more cash in the troughs at the price of a much longer tail. Neither structure is free, and neither result is guaranteed.
lessons.question: The owner asks which structure is 'safer' for a business with one strong season. What is the honest answer?
lessons.answer: They protect against different risks: the fixed schedule risks a winter payment the business must fund from reserves, while the share structure risks an obligation that stretches far beyond the season because collections slow when receipts fall.
lessons.distractor: The share structure is safer, because a payment that automatically falls with sales can never strain the business and the obligation always finishes on schedule.
lessons.correction: A percentage structure reduces the amount collected when sales fall, but the purchased amount does not shrink, so the schedule lengthens: in this illustration the remaining $40,892.31 would take about 63.3 weeks to collect in winter. Automatic adjustment in the payment is not automatic completion.

depth.definitions: Seasonality is a predictable pattern in receipts by period. A fixed schedule collects a stated amount on stated dates. A share-of-receipts structure collects a stated percentage of defined receipts, sometimes described as a holdback or split. An estimated term is the projected duration of a variable structure given assumptions about receipts. A reserve is cash set aside for a trough, and it must be funded from a surplus, not from the same receipts already committed to the obligation. Coverage is the ratio of available receipts to the scheduled collection in the same period. A tail is the part of the obligation that remains after the period the owner intended to finish by. A true-up is the reconciliation that reconciles estimated collections with the contractual percentage.
depth.mechanism: Start by plotting the merchant's receipts by week for at least twelve months, not by month, because a monthly average hides intra-month troughs where debits fall before deposits. Then overlay both structures. For the fixed version, compute the highest share of receipts the payment takes and identify the weeks where a reserve is required; the reserve must be funded from surplus weeks, which reduces the cash available for growth. For the share version, compute how the schedule lengthens as receipts fall, using three scenarios rather than one, and check whether the extended obligation collides with the next season's capital needs, with a renewal decision, or with a lease or loan ending. Consider a blended structure only if the contract genuinely provides it, and read who initiates any adjustment. Also test the merchant's ability to fund the trough at all: a business whose winter receipts are $8,076.92 a week and whose payroll alone exceeds that has a structural problem that no repayment structure solves. In that case a smaller obligation or a longer runway is the honest recommendation.
depth.secondExample: Consider a caterer whose receipts spike in November and December and fall by half in January. A 20-week fixed schedule starting in October collects heavily during the peak and finishes before the trough, which is duration-friendly; if the same schedule instead starts in January, the first eight weeks of collections land in the weakest period and would require the peak surplus as a reserve rather than as working capital. Now consider a share structure at 10% of receipts: in the peak months it collects more each week and shortens the schedule, so it converges on completion sooner, while in a weak year it stretches. The same product therefore behaves differently depending on the start date, which is a decision the merchant can sometimes influence. Comparing two offers without comparing start dates and receipt patterns produces a comparison of marketing material rather than of cash flows, and the offer documents may or may not permit a chosen start date.
depth.mistake: The polite version of the misleading pitch is 'the payment flexes with your sales, so slow months take care of themselves'. It confuses a smaller collection with a smaller obligation. Diagnose it by asking what the remaining total is after the slow period and how long it will take to collect at trough rates; if the answer is not known, the claim is unsupported. The opposite error is equally common: rejecting a share structure as inherently unsafe when for a business with steady, diversified receipts it may simply complete sooner. The judgement concerns this merchant's receipt pattern, this contract's definition of receipts and the merchant's ability to fund troughs, which is why neither structure can be declared universally better and no structure should be sold as guaranteeing that payments will always fit.
depth.application: Optional task: build a twelve-week overlay for a fictional seasonal merchant showing receipts, the fixed collection, the share-based collection and the resulting minimum weekly balance, then write the recommendation. Model response: 'On the fixed schedule your winter weeks pay 34.05% of receipts and require a $22,000 reserve from the peak, which is 45.83% of the proceeds you would receive. On an 8% share structure the winter collection is $646.15 a week and the remaining balance would take about 63 weeks at those rates, which collides with next spring's equipment purchase. Neither is obviously right, so we should size the obligation to a number that survives January on either calendar.' Self-review: weekly rather than monthly receipts; reserve funded from surplus; three receipt scenarios; both structures priced to completion; no claim that a structure guarantees affordability; provider approval not predicted.
depth.summary: Seasonality turns a repayment structure into a choice between two different risks. A fixed calendar concentrates the claim and requires reserves; a share structure spreads the claim and extends the tail. Neither is a promise, and the merchant's own weekly receipts decide the answer. Transfer the method to tourism, agriculture, retail and any business with a predictable trough: plot weekly receipts, test both structures to completion, and size the obligation so that the trough is survivable on either calendar.
